title: Inverse-Square Law
body:
Light from a source spreads over a sphere, and a sphere's area grows as $d^2$, so the light
collected per unit area falls as $1/d^2$.

$$
b = \frac{L}{4\pi d^2}
$$

where $b$ is apparent brightness, what a telescope measures, and $L$ is luminosity, what the
star actually emits.

```
same star at twice the distance   ->   one quarter as bright
same star at ten times            ->   one hundredth
```

Keeping the two quantities apart is the point. A bright-looking star is either genuinely
luminous or merely close, and apparent brightness alone cannot tell them apart, which is why
the night sky's brightest stars are a mixture of both.

The equation is used in both directions. With a distance from [[Stellar Parallax]], it
gives luminosity. With a luminosity known some other way, it gives distance, and a source whose
luminosity is known is a standard candle. Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae are the two
that matter, and they are what carried the distance ladder out to other galaxies and made
[[Hubble's Law]] measurable.
